Mice
mīs
n. pl. (small rodents; unclean under the law, and the figures cast in gold by the Philistines as a trespass offering)
Old English mys, plural of mus. The Hebrew 'akbar covers mice and rats generally; they are listed among the creeping things that are unclean.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The strangest offering in Scripture was made by pagans. The Philistines had taken the ark, and it had ruined them city by city — Dagon fallen and broken on his own threshold, the people smitten with emerods, the land marred by mice. Their priests and diviners advised them to send it home with a trespass offering: “Five golden emerods, and five golden mice, according to the number of the lords of the Philistines: for one plague was on you all, and on your lords” (1Sa 6:4). They were to make “images of your mice that mar the land; and ye shall give glory unto the God of Israel” (1Sa 6:5). So the coffer went beside the ark with the mice of gold in it (1Sa 6:11), and the golden mice were counted according to the number of all the cities (1Sa 6:18). Two lessons stand out. First, the heathen knew the hand that was on them and confessed it in gold. Second, they still handled the holy thing on their own terms — a new cart, kine that had never been yoked — and Israel afterward copied the cart, and Uzzah died. The ark judged those who took it and those who received it back, and God is not casual about His own holiness.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives mice as the plural of mouse, a small animal of the genus Mus, infesting houses and fields.

MICE, n. plu. of mouse.

MOUSE, n. A small animal of the genus Mus, inhabiting houses. The name is also applied to many other species of the genus.

In Scripture, an unclean creeping thing, and the figure cast in gold by the Philistines with the emerods.

Key Scripture

1Sa 6:11 — "And they laid the ark of the LORD upon the cart, and the coffer with the mice of gold and the images of their emerods."

Lev 11:29 — "These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind,"

Isa 66:17 — "They that sanctify themselves, and purify themselves in the gardens behind one tree in the midst, eating swine's flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together, saith the LORD."

Modern Corruption

The Philistines' golden mice are an unimprovable picture of a religion that acknowledges God's power, pays Him tribute, and still will not come to Him on His own terms.

expand to see more

The men of Ashdod, Gath and Ekron were not atheists. They had felt the hand of the God of Israel on their bodies and their fields for seven months, they said so publicly, and they paid in gold. Their diviners even preached a sermon out of Israel's history: wherefore then do ye harden your hearts, as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? What they would not do was submit. They sent the ark away rather than seek the God who owned it; they sent Him tribute rather than themselves. That arrangement has never gone out of fashion. It appears wherever God is acknowledged as real and powerful, credited with the blessings and blamed for the losses, offered money, ceremony, and public respect — and never obeyed. James calls the intellectual half of this the faith of devils, who believe and tremble. Isaiah 66:17 names the other half: people who sanctify and purify themselves in the gardens while eating the mouse and the swine, religion and abomination kept in the same house. The mercy of 1 Samuel 6 is that God took His own ark home; the warning of 1 Samuel 6:19 and of Uzzah is that He will be sanctified in them that come nigh Him, whether Philistine or Israelite.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'akbar (H5909), a mouse or field-rat; 'asham (H817), a trespass or guilt offering; sherets (H8318), a swarming or creeping thing.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'akbar (H5909) — a mouse, a field-rat; unclean in Leviticus, cast in gold by the Philistines, and eaten in the forbidden gardens of Isaiah 66; Leviticus 11:29, 1 Samuel 6:4, Isaiah 66:17.

Hebrew 'asham (H817) — a trespass offering, guilt and the payment for it; what the Philistines sent with the ark; 1 Samuel 6:3-4, Leviticus 5:15.

Hebrew sherets (H8318) — a swarming or creeping thing; the class of unclean creatures to which the mouse belongs; Leviticus 11:29-31.

Usage

"“Five golden emerods, and five golden mice” — the trespass offering of the Philistine lords."

"“Images of your mice that mar the land” — a confession cast in gold."

"“The abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together” — religion and abomination kept in one house."
